input:
Package 0.1: Commit the demo redesign and the test fix (2026-10-05).

What the package must deliver:
Two commits: the redesigned demo (docs/product-demo/**) and the intern test that no longer calls a live model. Done when git log shows the redesign, tests/test_intern.py patches the environment in setUp, and make rd-check passes.

The request: The demo was crowded and hard to read; make it clean, with an Overview per page and the details in tabs at the top, so a data scientist sees a calm product. Then commit the redesign and the fix for the two failing tests, and leave every other uncommitted file alone.

Plan the work.
output:
(1) What the package is for
The demo was crowded and hard to read; make it clean, with an Overview per page and the details in tabs at the top, so a data scientist sees a calm product. Then commit the redesign and the fix for the two failing tests, and leave every other uncommitted file alone.

(2) Plan
1. Split the demo's pages into four groups (workspace and knowledge, project flow A, project flow B, platform and plan) and restructure each into an Overview with four headline numbers and the details in top tabs.
2. Rebuild after each group and check every page for console errors with a headless browser, and compare screenshots.
3. Investigate the two failing tests reported by make rd-check before touching them.
4. Fix the intern test so it never reaches the developer's live model; leave the research-map test alone once its cause was known.
5. Run make rd-check, then commit the demo and the test fix as two separate commits, staging only those files.

(3) Decisions
- Every page opens on an Overview with four headline numbers and the one card that matters; details move into tabs with deep links (#view/tab). Because: The owner found the first demo crowded; a data scientist should see the state of a project at a glance and reach details on demand.
- Tours and the Blueprint 'Show on page' open the right tab by themselves. Because: Moving content into tabs would otherwise break the guided tours that point at it.
- The test clears the model key only for its own duration instead of changing .env or the app. Because: The bug was in the test's isolation, not in the product; the owner's .env must stay as it is.
- The research-map test was not changed. Because: It failed only because another session's work was half finished; once that session regenerated its files the test passed.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- The two failing tests may have different causes; fixing both in the product could hide that one fails only because another session's work is half finished.
- A test that builds the app reads the developer's .env, so it can reach a paid live model and pass or fail by machine rather than by code.
- Moving page sections into tabs can break the guided tours and the Blueprint 'Show on page' links that point at sections now inside a closed tab.
- A broad git add would sweep the owner's uncommitted recap and data files into the redesign commit.
- Four page groups restructured separately can drift into four slightly different layouts unless each is checked against the same design tokens and screenshots.

Package 0.1: Commit the demo redesign and the test fix (2026-10-05).

What the package must deliver:
Two commits: the redesigned demo (docs/product-demo/**) and the intern test that no longer calls a live model. Done when git log shows the redesign, tests/test_intern.py patches the environment in setUp, and make rd-check passes.

The change: docs/product-demo restructured: every page on an Overview plus top tabs, the sidebar regrouped as Workspace, Project, Knowledge and Platform, a new design system (cool grey ground, white cards, green actions, Inter and JetBrains Mono). tests/test_intern.py clears OPENAI_API_KEY for the duration of the API test so the intern follows its deterministic standard plan.

A finding (test, flaky): The intern API test sent a real request to OpenAI on a developer machine and failed there while CI stayed green.
How it shows: On a laptop with OPENAI_API_KEY in .env, the server loaded the key, the intern called the live model, the provider answered with a rate-limit error, the session ended 'failed' and the test went red; CI has no key, so it passed.

Diagnose and fix it.
output:
(1) Root cause
The server loads .env, and the test did not isolate itself from it.

(2) Why it matters
On any machine with a key in .env, each run of the suite sent a real request to the provider and went red whenever the provider rate-limited it, while CI stayed green. The owner saw make rd-check fail on a sound tree and could not tell a product regression from the provider's state. A test that fails by chance teaches people to ignore red results, and a real failure then hides among the false ones.

(3) The smallest fix
Clear the key in the test's setUp for its own duration so the intern always runs the standard plan, as in CI.
Set aside:
- Remove the key from .env or stop the server from loading it: set aside, because the owner's .env and the product were right; the test's isolation was the defect.

(4) The test that proves it
tests/test_intern.py: the API test now patches the environment and passes with or without a key on the machine.

(5) What stays open
Only this test was isolated. Any other test that builds the app still inherits the machine's .env, which is why later sessions run tests with DCLAB_NO_LIVE_MODELS=1.

Package 1.4: The page's data layer: API, live stream, polling (2026-10-05).

What the package must deliver:
DC.api (JSON, CSRF header from /api/config, one retry when the token is stale), DC.stream (server-sent events), DC.poll; the demo-only shared store removed; the blueprint layer and tours kept. Done when Home loads /api/workspace with no console error and a write after a server restart succeeds on the retry.

The request: The product's pages must talk to the real server: JSON calls with the request token, live events and polling, while pages not yet wired keep their sample data honestly labelled.

Plan the work.
output:
(1) What the package is for
The product's pages must talk to the real server: JSON calls with the request token, live events and polling, while pages not yet wired keep their sample data honestly labelled.

(2) Plan
1. Add DC.api, DC.stream and DC.poll to web/src/core.js.
2. Remove the demo-only window.claude decision store; keep localStorage.
3. Keep the blueprint layer and the tours.
4. Let a wired page call DC.markSample(false); unwired pages keep the 'Sample data' pill.
5. Exercise a write after restarting the server.

(3) Decisions
- Pages are wired phase by phase; an unwired page keeps its sample and says so. Because: A page half-filled with real and sample numbers would mislead; the pill tells the user which they see.
- The top-bar pill reads 'Your data' on a wired page instead of disappearing. Because: Saying positively what is shown is clearer than an absent label.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- The CSRF token is cached by the page and changes on every server restart, so every write from an open page fails until a reload.
- A page mixing real numbers and demo samples misleads unless each page says which it shows.
- Removing the demo's window.claude decision store breaks any page or tour that still calls it.
- A server-sent event stream that drops on a network blip leaves the page silently out of date unless it reconnects.
- Retrying a refused write could send a request twice if the first one had in fact been applied.

Package 1.4: The page's data layer: API, live stream, polling (2026-10-05).

What the package must deliver:
DC.api (JSON, CSRF header from /api/config, one retry when the token is stale), DC.stream (server-sent events), DC.poll; the demo-only shared store removed; the blueprint layer and tours kept. Done when Home loads /api/workspace with no console error and a write after a server restart succeeds on the retry.

The change: core.js gained the server helpers (api with the CSRF token, server-sent events, polling) and lost the artifact-only shared decision store; DC.markSample toggles the pill.

A finding (self, behaviour): After a server restart, an open page failed every action until it was reloaded.
How it shows: With the product open in the browser, the server restarted (a new request token); every write from the page was refused with 403 and kept failing until the user reloaded.

Diagnose and fix it.
output:
(1) Root cause
The page cached the token from its first load and never refreshed it.

(2) Why it matters
After any routine restart (a reload in development, a crash, a deploy), every save, upload or run from an open page failed with 403, and nothing on screen said a reload would fix it. To a user the product looked broken. It changes what DCLab does for a person without anyone deciding it: a result, a refusal or an artefact differs from what the person was promised, silently.

(3) The smallest fix
On a refused write the page fetches a fresh token from /api/config once and retries the request.

(4) The test that proves it
Checked in the browser after a restart while wiring the connectors.

(5) What stays open
Any 403 on a write is now retried once after fetching /api/config again, including a refusal for another reason, such as a role that may not make the move once sign-in arrived in 10.2. The second answer is the one shown, so the cost is one extra request, not a wrong result; reads are not retried.

Package 12.2: Configuration and secrets (2026-10-06).

What the package must deliver:
Every setting documented with a safe default and a test that fails when one is added without it; secrets from the environment or NAME_FILE files; the server and the worker refuse to start with a reason; DCLAB_ALLOWED_HOSTS for a proxy's names; a scan of the tracked files, the history and the image that never prints a value.

The request: Document every setting in .env.example with a safe default. Keys and connection strings come from the environment or Docker secrets, never from a committed file or an image layer. Fail at start with a clear message when a required setting is missing or the database cannot be reached. Add the allowed host names as a setting for the host check. Scan the repository and the image for committed secrets and report what was found.

Plan the work.
output:
(1) What the package is for
Document every setting in .env.example with a safe default. Keys and connection strings come from the environment or Docker secrets, never from a committed file or an image layer. Fail at start with a clear message when a required setting is missing or the database cannot be reached. Add the allowed host names as a setting for the host check. Scan the repository and the image for committed secrets and report what was found.

(2) Plan
1. List every setting the code and scripts read that .env.example does not document, see what each does, and write them in with safe defaults.
2. Read secrets from NAME_FILE files, add the allowed-hosts setting, and a problems() check the server and the worker run at start.
3. Write scripts/scan_secrets.py for the tracked files and, because a secret committed once and deleted later stays in git, for every commit in the history; verify the history scan really read the history (its first result was suspiciously clean).
4. Write tests/test_config.py, including a test that every setting read in the code is documented.
5. Run make check-all and the reviewer; fix all thirteen findings; re-check; fix the last note; gate again and commit.

(3) Decisions
- Secret files are read by a small dependency-free module loaded when the package is imported, leniently there and strictly in Settings.load. Because: The storage and accounts commands, the MCP server and the model command-line tools never call Settings.load; only an import-time load reaches every entry point, and the strict load lets the server refuse to start on an unreadable file.
- Only an allowed list of names can be set from a file: the product's own keys, DCLAB_DB_<NAME> and DCLAB_TIER_<TIER>_API_KEY. Because: AWS defines its own _FILE variables (shared credentials, config, web identity token) with a different meaning; a prefix rule broke start-up and copied whole credential files into stray variables.
- The scanner reports where, the kind and a short hash of the value, never the value; the allow-list matches by path, kind and value hash. Because: A scan log is itself a place a secret can leak, and an allow-list by path and kind alone would hide any later real secret of the same kind in the same file.
- An unknown DCLAB_AUTH value, and allowed host names with sign-in off, refuse to start. Because: A typo such as 'passwd' fell back to no sign-in; with a proxy's host names allowed, that would leave a server open to the network.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- A nested .env with a real key can reach an image layer, because Docker's ignore patterns do not behave like git's.
- Secrets read from files in one entry point but not in the others leave the command-line tools blind to them.
- A lenient parser that maps an unknown value to the default fails open: a mistyped sign-in mode means no sign-in.
- A secrets scanner that filters placeholders by line, or allow-lists by file, hides real keys next to harmless ones.
- The test that says every setting is documented is only as wide as its pattern and its folders.

(5) How you will know it is done
- secrets scan: No secret in the tracked files or in any line added in the history, apart from allow-listed made-up test values.

Answer with exactly these parts: (1) Findings, most severe first, each with its severity, the concrete scenario (inputs, then the wrong result), why it matters, and the fix you would ask for; (2) Verdict.
input:
Package 12.2: Configuration and secrets (2026-10-06).

What the package must deliver:
Every setting documented with a safe default and a test that fails when one is added without it; secrets from the environment or NAME_FILE files; the server and the worker refuse to start with a reason; DCLAB_ALLOWED_HOSTS for a proxy's names; a scan of the tracked files, the history and the image that never prints a value.

The change: Every setting documented in .env.example; dclab_rnd/secret_files.py reads NAME_FILE secrets; settings.py gains allowed_hosts and hosts() and problems() (start-up checks on the database, the schema head, sign-in settings and numbers); the server and the worker refuse to start with a reason; lenient number parsing in the database pool and the gateway; scripts/scan_secrets.py and make scan-secrets over the tracked files and the history; tests/test_config.py.

Review it.
output:
(1) Findings
- F1 [privacy] A real key in a nested .env file would have been copied into the image.
  Scenario: dclab_rnd/agentic/.env (git-ignored) holds a non-empty model key and a TabPFN token; .dockerignore's .env and .env.* match only at the root of the build context, and the Dockerfile's COPY . /app would have put the file in an image layer on make up.
  Why it matters: The first make up would have put a working model key and a TabPFN token into an image layer; anyone with the image could have read them and spent on the owner's account, and the only remedy then is to revoke the keys.
  Fix to ask for: Exclude **/.env and **/.env.* (keeping !.env.example) and .git. Both of the day's builds had failed before the copy step, and their cache was deleted, so no image held the key and it did not need rotating.
- F7 [privacy] The scanner's placeholder filter skipped whole lines.
  Scenario: A made-up key on a notebook line that also holds a URL containing 'example', or a YAML key followed by '# put your own here', was reported clean: any line containing 'example', 'your ' or 'xxx' hid a real key.
  Why it matters: A real key on a line that also held the word 'example', common in notebooks and config comments, was reported clean, so the scan gave a false all-clear in exactly the files where keys are pasted by hand.
  Fix to ask for: Placeholders are checked against the matched text only.
- F8 [privacy] The history allow-list keyed on path and kind only.
  Scenario: A real database URL with a password added later to tests/test_connectors.py would be hidden, because a made-up one of the same kind in that file was allowed.
  Why it matters: Once one made-up database URL in a test file was allowed, any real URL with a password added to that file later would have been hidden for good, in both the file scan and the history scan.
  Fix to ask for: Entries are path, kind and a short hash of the value, used in both modes.
- F2 [behaviour] NAME_FILE secrets were ignored outside Settings.load.
  Scenario: With only DCLAB_DATABASE_URL_FILE set (the example in .env.example), python -m dclab_rnd.storage status printed 'DCLAB_DATABASE_URL is not set' and exited 2; the Dockerfile's 'storage upgrade && uvicorn' would never start the server, and accounts add said accounts need PostgreSQL.
  Why it matters: A deployment that followed .env.example and gave the database URL as a file would never have started: the container's migrate-then-serve command failed at the migrate step, and the accounts tool claimed PostgreSQL was missing. The documented way to keep secrets out of the environment was the one way that did not work.
  Fix to ask for: Move the loading into dclab_rnd/secret_files.py, imported by the package itself, so every entry point sees the secrets.
- F3 [behaviour] The AWS_ prefix for secret files was too broad.
  Scenario: AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE pointing at a missing file made Settings.load raise, so the server, the worker and the limits all failed, although boto3 accepts a missing file; a readable one copied the whole credentials file into a stray variable every subprocess inherits.
  Why it matters: An operator with a normal AWS setup pointing at a missing credentials file would have had the server, the worker and the limits refuse to start, though AWS's own library accepts that; with a readable file, the whole credentials file was copied into a variable every subprocess inherits.
  Fix to ask for: An allowed list of target names; AWS's own _FILE variables are left alone.
- F4 [behaviour] Settings appeared as database connections on Home.
  Scenario: With DCLAB_DB_POOL_SIZE=10 (newly documented) and DCLAB_DB_WAREHOUSE_FILE set, connections() returned pool_size and warehouse_file as two connections.
  Why it matters: The Home page would have offered 'pool_size' and 'warehouse_file' as databases to import from, the moment someone set the newly documented pool size or a connection's password file; choosing one would fail with a confusing error.
  Fix to ask for: connections() skips names ending in _FILE, POOL_SIZE, MAX_OVERFLOW and PASSWORD.
- F5 [behaviour] The numeric check covered only four settings.
  Scenario: DCLAB_PORT=abc silently became 8765, DCLAB_WORKER_THREADS=abc became 4, and DCLAB_WORKSPACE_MONTHLY_EUR=20€ was read as no limit by the limits but made the gateway raise ValueError on every model request.
  Why it matters: A typo in a port or a thread count was silently replaced by the default, so the server listened somewhere other than the operator wrote; a budget written as '20€' meant no limit in one place and a ValueError on every model request in another.
  Fix to ask for: The check covers ports, threads, the stale seconds, the MCP port, both budgets and every DCLAB_LIMIT_*.
- F6 [behaviour] An unknown DCLAB_AUTH value failed open.
  Scenario: DCLAB_AUTH=passwd (or sso, or true) became none with no message, so every request was treated as the local owner; with DCLAB_ALLOWED_HOSTS now letting a proxy through, the server would be open.
  Why it matters: An operator who wrote a plausible but unknown sign-in mode got no sign-in at all, with every request treated as the owner; with the new allowed-hosts setting letting a proxy through, that is an open server on the network, reached by a typo.
  Fix to ask for: problems() reads the raw value and refuses an unknown mode, and refuses allowed host names with sign-in off.
- F11 [behaviour] Allowed host names were not normalised.
  Scenario: DCLAB_ALLOWED_HOSTS=dclab.example.com:8443, https://dclab.example.com or DCLab.example.com never matched (Starlette strips the port and compares case-sensitively), so every request got 400; 'dclab.*' tripped an assert inside create_app.
  Why it matters: An operator who wrote the proxy's host name with a port, a scheme or a capital letter got a 400 on every request and no hint why; a wildcard like 'dclab.*' crashed app start-up on an assert instead of giving a readable refusal.
  Fix to ask for: hosts() lowercases and strips the scheme and port; problems() rejects bad wildcards; '*' alone is dropped and reported.
- N1 [latent] A NAME_FILE written in .env was missed by the accounts tool.
  Scenario: The import-time load runs before load_dotenv; the server and worker still pick it up through Settings.load, but accounts add calls the database URL right after load_dotenv and misses it.
  Why it matters: An operator who wrote the database URL as a file path inside .env, rather than in the real environment, would find that 'accounts add' could not see the database while the server could; making the first owner would fail.
  Fix to ask for: The accounts and storage tools load secret files again after reading .env.
- F9 [gap] The 'every setting is documented' test had blind spots.
  Scenario: Its pattern could not match KAGGLE_CONFIG_DIR, had no AWS_ prefix, did not scan scripts/ (three DCLAB_CHAT_UI and notebook settings undocumented) or docker-compose.yml (DCLAB_DB_PASSWORD), and exempted the whole DCLAB_DB_ family.
  Why it matters: The test that promises every setting is documented would have passed while settings in scripts, in the compose file and in the whole DCLAB_DB_ family were missing from .env.example, so an operator would not learn they exist.
  Fix to ask for: [A-Z0-9_]+ for every prefix, AWS_ and HF_ added, scripts/ and the Docker files scanned (tracked files only), and only names ending in '_' exempt.
- F12 [gap] A sentence on the platform page became false.
  Scenario: The page said the server answers only on 127.0.0.1 and localhost, which is wrong once DCLAB_ALLOWED_HOSTS is set.
  Why it matters: The platform page would have told an operator the server answers only on this machine while it was in fact serving a proxy's host names, which is the wrong thing to believe about exposure.
  Fix to ask for: The sentence is built from the real setting.
- F13 [gap] Several refusals were untested.
  Scenario: Nothing tested the 'schema behind the code' refusal, the worker's refusal (it should return 2 and print 'cannot start'), or a _FILE secret reaching an entry point.
  Why it matters: The refusals that protect a deployment (a schema behind the code, a worker with bad settings, a secret given as a file) could have stopped working with the suite still green.
  Fix to ask for: Tests for each; the PostgreSQL-backed ones ran in the re-check without being skipped.
- F10 [flaky] The scan crashed on a tracked file deleted from the working tree.
  Scenario: A tracked file removed without git rm made path.stat() raise FileNotFoundError, so the secrets test errored during ordinary uncommitted work.
  Why it matters: Anyone deleting a tracked file during ordinary work, before committing the removal, got an error from the secrets test; a test that errors on routine work gets skipped, and then it no longer guards anything.
  Fix to ask for: Skip a path that is not a file.

(2) Verdict
FAIL: 14 findings to fix before this change is committed.

(1) Findings
- F1 [behaviour] Metric labels could grow without bound through the HTTP method.
  Scenario: The image runs uvicorn on h11, which accepts any token as a method; 50 requests with random methods such as XABC12 added 150 new series, each answered 403, with no sign-in needed, so anyone could grow the process's memory and Prometheus's series.
  Why it matters: Anyone on the network, without signing in, could send requests with made-up methods and add new metric series without limit, growing the app's memory and the monitoring system's storage until one of them fell over; each request was refused, so nothing in the access rules would have stopped it.

- F2 [behaviour] A busy or invalid metrics port stopped the app or the worker from starting.
  Scenario: A developer sets DCLAB_METRICS_PORT=9464 in .env as .env.example suggests; the server and a separate worker both load it and collide, and the worker dies with 'Address already in use'; every parallel test process also loads .env and runs a lifespan, so every test file after the first fails to start its app. DCLAB_METRICS_PORT=abc raised a raw ValueError.

  Fix to ask for: Wrap the bind in try/except OSError and log that metrics are off; check the value as an integer port in problems().
- F3 [behaviour] Counters lost precision after six digits.
  Scenario: A token counter at 123456789 rendered as 1.23457e+08; token counts reach millions within days and probe counts within weeks, after which rate() and increase() move in steps of 10, 100, 1000.

  Fix to ask for: Render with full precision (repr of the float).
- F4 [behaviour] A 500 response carried no request id.
  Scenario: A route raising ValueError, called with X-Request-ID: trace-err-0001, returned 500 without the header: the error middleware outside this middleware built the response. Errors are when a person most needs an id to quote.
  Why it matters: A person who hit a server error had no request id to quote, so support could not find the one log line that explains the failure; errors are exactly when that id is needed.
  Fix to ask for: Catch the exception in the middleware, log the line and return a JSON 500 with the request id in the body and the header.
- F5 [gap] A dead worker's jobs were never counted as failures.
  Scenario: The worker container is killed for memory while running a stage; another process's recover() marks the job interrupted, but dclab_jobs_total and dclab_job_failures_total do not move and nothing is logged, though this is the failure an alert most needs.

  Fix to ask for: recover() counts the job as interrupted with its time and writes the 'job ended' line.
- F6 [gap] A 429's log line had no person or workspace.

  Why it matters: When someone was rate-limited, the log line could not say who or which workspace, so an operator could neither tell the person nor see whether one script was hammering the service.
  Fix to ask for: Set it right after the person is identified.
- F7 [gap] Plain-text mode printed an empty line per request.
  Scenario: Without DCLAB_LOG_FORMAT=json (the default for make notebook, make dev and make test) every request, including the Compute page's 2.5-second poll, printed a bare 'INFO dclab request' with no route, status or id, flooding the output the parallel runner prints for a failing file.
  Why it matters: In the default plain mode every request, including the Compute page's poll every 2.5 seconds, printed a line that said nothing, burying a failing test's real output under noise in the runner's report.
  Fix to ask for: Plain text logs only server errors, with the same fields.

FAIL: 7 findings to fix before this change is committed.

(1) What the package is for
The pages wrote 98 request paths by hand, so a renamed route or a missing parameter only showed up as a 404 in someone's browser, and each page said 'could not load' in its own way. Generate one API client from the server's OpenAPI schema into the frontend's api.js and make every view use it; give every view the same loading, empty and failed states with existing components; a signed-out answer sends the user to sign-in; change no layout, colour or wording that already exists.

(2) Plan
1. Measure how views call the API today (98 calls) and check that the server's route function names are unique enough to name the client's functions.
2. Write the generator (dclab_rnd/agentic/web/client.py): read the schema from the app, recover each function name from FastAPI's operationId (included routers do not show as plain routes), emit JSDoc-typed functions with path parameters encoded and required and unknown query parameters refused at run time.
3. Rewrite the 98 call sites with a codemod that matches each path against the routes and prints what it cannot convert; convert the two left (the audit page's built-up filters and Compute's action links) by hand; add DC.client.path and href for the event streams and downloads.
4. Make make web regenerate api.js and the build's --check fail when it is stale.
5. Build DC.states from the existing empty component and warning callout; track each page's load to show Loading… when slow and the failure with Try again.
6. Write tests; check all 19 pages in a real browser on a throwaway workspace on files (never the development database), then with one read made to fail.
7. Run make check-all and the reviewer; fix the three findings, re-check in the browser, re-review; commit the separate CI test fix on its own, then 13.1.

(3) Decisions
- Name each client function after the route's Python function. Because: The names were unique and read well (DC.client.getProject(id)), and they stay stable when a path changes.
- Rewrite the call sites with a codemod that refuses what it cannot match. Because: 98 hand edits invite silent mistakes in method, parameter order or encoding; a codemod checked against the route table converts the plain cases exactly and lists the rest.
- Generating the client builds a server on a scratch folder on files, and importing the server no longer builds its app (made on first use). Because: The build runs in rd-check on every machine; it must work with the database stopped and must never open the owner's workspace or database.
- A page's failure is credited only to the page that started the request. Because: Polls and slow reads from a page just left would otherwise put another page's error on the current one.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Generating a client from the OpenAPI schema means importing the server; if importing builds an app, a build step touches the real database and settings.

- A page-level loading tracker sees only what a page's enter returns; pages that start reads without returning them stay silent on failure.
- Requests that outlive their page (polls) can report their failure on whatever page is current.
- The owner asked for no change to layout, colour or wording, so the new states must reuse existing components exactly.

A finding (reviewer, behaviour): A failure could be shown on the wrong page, and an old banner stayed up while a page reloaded.

(1) Root cause
A failure was credited to whichever watch was current when it arrived, and track() never hid the box when it started.

A person could see 'Part of this page could not be loaded' on Lab for a failure that belonged to Home, or keep seeing an old banner on a page that had loaded fine, so the one signal meant to say what failed pointed at the wrong page. It changes what DCLab does for a person without anyone deciding it: a result, a refusal or an artefact differs from what the person was promised, silently.

(3) The smallest fix
api() takes the watch when the request starts and only if it belongs to the current view; enterView clears the watch when enter returns no promise; track() hides the box first.

(4) The test that proves it
Checked in the browser: a slow page left, then a failing read elsewhere.

A poll started by another page, such as Brief's, can still count against the page that is loading.

input:
Package 14.3: A frozen benchmark of 100 or more unseen cases (2026-10-07).

What the package must deliver:
dclab_rnd/agent_eval/benchmark.py (make benchmark): 100+ cases (60+ sealed) from new generators and scikit-learn's bundled tables; trap families from docs/SYSTEM_EVALUATION.md plus clean controls; dev and sealed test split, fingerprints committed and checked by a test; scripted policies scored on both sets per family with Wilson intervals and stored as evidence.

The request: The judgment suite's 20 cases were written alongside the prompts, so its scores cannot say how DCLab does on tables it has never seen. After writing Part 3 (prove it works) into the playbook, build a frozen benchmark: 100 or more seeded cases from bases no prompt was tuned on, each with a prediction moment, at most one planted trap and the decisions a careful data scientist would accept, split into a dev set and a sealed test set whose fingerprints are committed; score the scripted policies on both, per family, with Wilson intervals; never tune on the sealed set.

Plan the work.
output:
(1) What the package is for
The judgment suite's 20 cases were written alongside the prompts, so its scores cannot say how DCLab does on tables it has never seen. After writing Part 3 (prove it works) into the playbook, build a frozen benchmark: 100 or more seeded cases from bases no prompt was tuned on, each with a prediction moment, at most one planted trap and the decisions a careful data scientist would accept, split into a dev set and a sealed test set whose fingerprints are committed; score the scripted policies on both, per family, with Wilson intervals; never tune on the sealed set.

(2) Plan
1. Propose Part 3 to the owner (inputs, live models, frozen benchmark, users, staging, policy model); on the owner's yes, write it into the playbook as packages 14.1 to 14.8 and push.
2. Read the judgment suite's scorer and runner so the benchmark reuses them.
3. Write base generators (claims, subscriptions and demand for dev; loans, readmissions, sensors and the diabetes and wine tables shipped with scikit-learn for test), plant at most one trap per case, add clean controls, and split by base so no base is in both sets.
4. Generate: 95 cases with 57 sealed fell short of the package's 100 and 60, so add one more held-out generator (late deliveries) for 108 cases, 38 dev and 70 sealed.
5. Commit the sealed fingerprints; write tests for size, the split by source, unique seeds and unchanged fingerprints.
6. Run the scripted policies on both sets and record them as BEN-001 (dev) and BEN-002 (sealed).
7. Run the reviewer; fix its findings; make check-all; commit together with 14.2.

(3) Decisions
- Split dev and test by base table, not by case. Because: Cases from one base share columns and a generator; splitting by base keeps the sealed set genuinely unseen.
- Include two real public tables that ship with scikit-learn in the sealed set. Because: They need no download and are not shaped by the author's generators.
- A run on the sealed set is always recorded, and an existing result file is refused before the run, not after. Because: An unrecorded look at the sealed set is tuning by memory; refusing afterwards would already have shown the scores.
- A weakness found in one sealed family is written down, not fixed. Because: The sealed set had already been scored; renaming its columns now would be tuning on it. It waits for a new benchmark version.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Cases written by the same person who wrote the prompts and the audit can carry telling names that measure luck rather than judgment.
- A sealed set is only sealed if every look at it is recorded; a run that prints scores and fails to write leaves an unrecorded look.
- Fingerprints must be the same on every machine and pandas version, or the 'unchanged' check fails falsely on CI.
- Cases that share a base table are not independent, so the intervals can look tighter than the evidence is.
- The size the package asked for (100 cases, 60 sealed) must be met by adding bases, not by lowering the bar.

(5) How you will know it is done
- scripted policies on the sealed set (BEN-002): Score each scripted policy on the 70 sealed cases per family with Wilson intervals; record every run (no pass threshold yet: the gate is 14.5's).

The request: The challenge's rubric asked for an API with Flask and Gunicorn, Docker and tests. Next to the notebook export, export a finished project as a scoring service that computes the same features as training and holds no data.

output:
(1) What the package is for
The challenge's rubric asked for an API with Flask and Gunicorn, Docker and tests. Next to the notebook export, export a finished project as a scoring service that computes the same features as training and holds no data.

(2) Plan
1. Write studio/service.py: refuse a project whose final stage is not approved; refit through runner.fit_and_predict, which now returns the fitted recipe.
2. Strip the pickle of data: replace the bundle by its spec, drop per-row rates, hash category levels, feature names, entity values and places.
3. Vendor the code the scorer needs and write app.py, scorer.py, requirements, a Dockerfile copying no data and tests on made-up rows.
4. Test that the exported scorer, run in a Python that cannot import the repository, gives the engine's predictions, and that no row value is in the export.
5. Run the export's own tests once in a clean Python 3.12 environment.
6. Fix the review's findings; mark the package done in part.

(3) Decisions
- The service computes behaviour features within each request; a single row is told it has no history. Because: The engine measured the model with features computed within each fold; storing training-period history in the service would make served features differ from the evaluated ones. The stateful service is recorded as open.
- The hashing key is never in the exported folder; the service reads it at serve time (DCLAB_SERVICE_KEY). Because: A salt pickled next to the hashes lets anyone enumerate phone numbers or grid cells and recover them.
- The export refuses a refit that does not reproduce the approved holdout score. Because: The served model must be the approved one; a refit that scores differently is a different model.
- The service gives an alert only at a stated budget. Because: The plan says the threshold is chosen with the person; without a budget the service returns scores.

- Row values (phone numbers, ids, places) surviving inside fitted encoders, count tables or detectors, and so travelling in model.pkl.
- Served features that differ from the evaluated ones: behaviour counts that depend on which rows share a request, column types inferred per request, missing keys normalised differently at fit and at serve.
- A refit at export time that is not the model the person approved, unnoticed because a parity test compares a refit with itself.
- A service built from a project no person approved, or raising alerts at a threshold the person never chose.
- Review changes such as a log target or clipping applied in training and forgotten by the scorer.

(5) How you will know it is done
- service parity with the engine: The service's predictions equal the engine's on the replica's holdout, in a Python that cannot import the repository, with no row value in the export.
- the export's own tests: The generated tests pass in a clean environment (Done-when of 15.10).
- the Docker image in the end-to-end flows: The image runs in make product-e2e (Done-when of 15.10).

  Fix to ask for: Write the review operations and the target range into model.json and apply them in the scorer.

- F13 [gap] The service gave an alert at a threshold the person never chose.
  Scenario: It emitted 'alert' at the task assessment's threshold, while the plan says the threshold is chosen with the person.
  Why it matters: The service would have raised alerts at a threshold DCLab picked, so a team would staff reviews around an alert rate nobody agreed to.
  Fix to ask for: An alert only at a stated budget; otherwise scores.

(2) Verdict
FAIL: 8 findings to fix before this change is committed.

Let DCLab solve recommendation problems: which items to show each user next, from views and purchases with time.

1. Cut every user at one recommendation moment; models read only the interactions up to it and the items created by it.

Package 16.9: Decisions on top of a model: thresholds, prices, budgets (2026-10-13).

What the package must deliver:
A decision layer for any kind that predicts: from the stated value and cost of an action, the threshold, review budget or price that maximises expected value on out-of-fold predictions, with an interval and a stated assumption about how the outcome responds; prices from a model of acceptance by price, with a warning when prices did not vary. Done when the fraud replica gets a budget from the review cost, a pricing replica gets a price curve with an interval, and a fixed-price replica gets the cannot-learn warning.

The request: A model ranks or predicts, but a team acts: choose the review budget or the price that is worth most, from what the action is worth and what it costs, so that challenge mode can answer a pricing question with numbers.

Plan the work.
output:
(1) What the package is for
A model ranks or predicts, but a team acts: choose the review budget or the price that is worth most, from what the action is worth and what it costs, so that challenge mode can answer a pricing question with numbers.

(2) Plan
1. Write the pure core in dclab_core/decide.py: review_budget on out-of-fold scores with a bootstrap over rows or entities, and price_curve with price_variation.
2. Write a pricing replica with a known true best price: fees offered to couriers, varied at random, or set by a formula of distance and hour.
3. Check the core on both versions before wiring anything: the varied market's interval should hold the true best, the formula market should be refused.
4. Give the solution a typed decision (review or price) and compute it in the final stage, with a claim whose numbers all come from evidence.decision.
5. Render it in the traced report and let challenge mode deliver a stated decision; bump dclab_core to 0.3.0 and check the wheel in a clean Python.
6. Review, fix, rd-check, record.

(3) Decisions
- The review budget is chosen on out-of-fold scores of the training rows and read once on the holdout. Because: Choosing on the holdout would make its score optimistic; the holdout is for the honest number after the choice.
- The price is chosen on the training rows only; the holdout is not read for it. Because: The holdout holds no counterfactual prices, so it cannot check a price that was never offered; reading it would add nothing but a temptation.
- Acceptance is modelled as logistic in the log of the price against its reference, plus the context, inside folds. Because: A monotone, simple response that extrapolates nowhere: the curve is read only within the 5th to 95th percentile of the multiples seen, and a best price at the edge is flagged.
- Refuse to draw a curve when prices were not varied, and say why. Because: A price set by a formula of the context cannot be told apart from the context's own effect; a confident curve there would be a confounded guess.
- Both selling and paying are supported. Because: The challenge shape is a fee paid to a courier (acceptance rises with the price, the margin is value minus price), the classic shape is a price charged to a customer.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- A column the decision reads, such as the reference price or the unit value, is not checked against the prediction moment, and a post-outcome value enters the acceptance model.
- A price set by a rule of the context looks varied, and a confounded curve is drawn with a confident interval.
- The holdout is used to choose the budget or the price, so the number reported on it is optimistic.
- Missing or zero prices crash the decision, or produce a margin of None that reads like a result.
- A new report rule for price words takes over requirements that only mention a price, such as predicting house prices.

(5) How you will know it is done
- price curve on the varied pricing replica: The 90% bootstrap interval of the best multiple holds the replica's true best multiple (Done when, fixed with the package).
- formula-priced replica: No curve; the cannot-learn warning with its reasons.
- fraud review budget from the review cost: A share chosen from value 60 per case and 1.5 per review, interval over bikers, lower-bound note with partial labels, holdout read after the choice.

Review it.
output:
(1) Findings
- R1 [leakage] A forbidden column could become an input of the acceptance model.
  Scenario: Forbidden final_customer_fare plus a price decision with reference_column final_customer_fare: validation passed and the model was fitted on a post-outcome column through log(price/reference).
  Why it matters: A person who forbade final_customer_fare but named it as the reference price would get a price curve fitted on a value known only after the ride. The best fee and its interval would look precise and be unusable at offer time.
  Fix to ask for: A column the decision reads can never be forbidden (Solution refuses it), and the engine refuses a price or reference that is not an input, and a unit value that is blocked, naming each role.
- R3 [leakage] A price set by a categorical formula passed as varied, and a confounded curve was drawn.
  Scenario: price = tariff[zone] with zone a string that also drives acceptance, and price with no effect: the numeric-only check found R2 -0.07 and drew a best multiple of 1.18 with interval [1.18, 1.18].
  Why it matters: Surge pricing by zone or weather, a common real case, would pass as varied: the reviewer's probe drew a best multiple of 1.18 with a zero-width interval, although the price had no effect on acceptance.
  Fix to ask for: Low-cardinality categories enter the check as codes and the acceptance model one-hot encoded inside its folds.
- R2 [behaviour] A real randomised price test was refused as a formula when its arm was logged.
  Scenario: The varied replica plus a column test_arm = fee / usual_fee: the check said the other columns explain 100% of the price and asked the person to run the very test they ran.
  Why it matters: A team that ran a real randomised fee test and logged its arm would be told its prices came from a formula and asked to run the test it had already run. The one kind of data that can answer a pricing question would be refused.
  Fix to ask for: The decision can name test_arm_columns, which are left out of the check and the context; the warning names the columns that explain the price so a person can tell an arm from a formula.
- R4 [behaviour] Missing or zero values crashed the decision, or gave a margin of None.
  Scenario: One NaN price or a zero reference raised inside the formula check; a unit value filled only for accepted offers gave learnable True, the best multiple at the lowest edge and 'an expected margin of None per offer'.
  Why it matters: Data where the unit value is filled only for accepted offers would get a best price at the lowest edge and a claim of an expected margin of None per offer. A single missing price would end the decision with a bare ValueError.
  Fix to ask for: Rows without a positive finite price, reference or value are left out and counted; context columns that are entirely missing are dropped and the rest imputed inside folds; a value missing on more than 5% of rows is refused with the reason.
- R5 [behaviour] A price word in a requirement hid a model's job in the deliverables map.
  Scenario: 'Predict house prices', 'Predict which transactions are charged back' and 'Use the customer feedback to improve the model' became 'not covered' because the new price rule matched first ('fee' also matched 'feedback').
  Why it matters: A house-price regression challenge would show its main requirement as not covered, and a requirement about customer feedback would lose its link to the model. The report would look incomplete exactly where DCLab had done the work.
  Fix to ask for: The price rule answers only when a decision record was read, otherwise the next rules answer; 'fee' is matched as a whole word.
- R6 [behaviour] A review budget that pays nothing read as a recommendation.
  Scenario: The claim said 'Reviewing the riskiest 0.00% of rows maximises expected value at 0.0 per row', and the 'no review pays' note was in neither the claim nor the report.
  Why it matters: A team whose reviews cost more than they recover would read 'reviewing the riskiest 0.00% maximises expected value' as advice to act, when the honest answer is that no review pays.
  Fix to ask for: When no review pays, the claim is a risk that says so, and the report writes the note.
- R7 [latent] The price interval ignored entities.
  Scenario: Couriers who see many offers: folds and the bootstrap resampled rows, so the interval was too narrow, unlike the review budget's entity bootstrap.
  Why it matters: With couriers who each see many offers, the price interval would be too narrow, so the chosen fee would look more certain than the data allows. The review budget already bootstrapped over entities, so the two decisions disagreed about how much the data says.
  Fix to ask for: The group column reaches price_curve: grouped stratified folds and an entity bootstrap.
- R8 [gap] The new end-to-end challenge test would error where pandas is missing.
  Scenario: It sat in a class without the skip guard, so the agent environment would error on the import.
  Why it matters: In the agent environment, which has no pandas, the new challenge test would error instead of skipping, turning the suite red for a reason unrelated to the code.
  Fix to ask for: Moved into the class that skips when dependencies are missing.

(2) Verdict
FAIL: 8 findings to fix before this change is committed.

(1) What the package is for
The owner wants more AI, agents and LLMs inside the workflow: to understand problems better, build better workflows and make better decisions. Start with one contract every model role follows, inside the portable core, so DCLab's main product can run the same roles through its own gateway.

(2) Plan
1. Write Part 7 of the playbook first: the roles at the workflow's steps (analyst, investigator, planner, feature engineer, critic, reporter), each with a deterministic fallback, a versioned prompt in dclab_core and a gate it must pass before it is on by default.
2. Read how the R&D repository already keeps prompts as hashed files (dclab_rnd/prompts, package A4.3) and reproduce the idea in dclab_core without importing dclab_rnd.
3. Write dclab_core/prompts (text, names, fingerprints, HASHES.json and a --record entry point) and add the agents and prompts subpackages and the .md files to the wheel.
4. Write Role, RoleResult, run_role and ScriptedAdvisor in dclab_core/agents: run_role computes the fallback first and returns the advisor's output only after the role's parser accepts it.
5. Write tests/test_core_agents.py: an accepted answer is used and said so; no advisor, an abstention, a failure and a refused answer all give the fallback; rows in the evidence raise; every prompt is pinned and ships in the wheel.
6. Move 17.2's problem-analyst hook in understand onto the contract (PROBLEM_ANALYST with its evidence and parser, run through run_role with its pinned prompt).

- A role returns its output with its source (advisor or fallback) and the reason (no advisor, abstained, failed, invalid). Because: DCLab must work with the model off, and every record must say whether a value came from a model or from the rules.
- Prompts are files in dclab_core pinned by HASHES.json; a changed prompt fails a test until its hash is recorded. Because: The main product sends the same words through its own gateway, and recording a new hash is the moment the role must be measured again.

- A role's fallback differs from the rules' old behaviour, so understand() changes its answers for everyone running with no model.

- A parser accepts an answer that code cannot check, and a model's free text lands in a field as if it were validated.

(1) What the package is for
First, store everything users do in DCLab and everything DCLab does in reply, organized and findable, to improve the system and to train the owner's model; adoptable by the main product.

(2) Plan
1. Inventory what the studio records (14 mechanisms, no shared session or user id) and read the main product's tables at one commit.

- The contract is an exchange format; each host keeps its stores. Because: The main product's rules forbid a parallel system and it already has append-only agent events, invocations, decisions and run events.

- Values exported as metadata.
- Real text refused as a credential.
- A product's sessions read wrongly.

Package 19.8: Labels from every source: planted truth, measurements, people who chose otherwise, and blind reviewers with known weights (2026-10-14).

Benchmark labels for decisions on replicas, measured labels (a leak's lift, a split's optimism), person labels from overrides (user_decision_exposed), and a blind labelling page on a sample drawn with known probabilities; the precedence blind, benchmark, measured, exposed as one function.

output:
(1) What the package is for
The owner wants decision models trained on DCLab's decisions; a decision without a label of what was right teaches nothing.

(2) Plan
1. The precedence and the blind draw in dclab_core, so both hosts weigh labels the same way.
2. Benchmark labels from a replica's declared traps after an acceptance run; exposed labels where a person was shown the rule's answer; measured labels where the leakage stage measures.
3. Routes and an Admin tab: the ledger's counts and blind labelling, for the owner and reviewers.
4. Review, plant faults, fix.

(3) Decisions
- An exposed label counts only when it contradicts an answer a rule or a model gave. Because: A person who saw the answer and agreed is not evidence it was right (the main product's rule: demote, never promote).
- Only planted traps are labelled on a replica, never 'not a leak' for the other columns. Because: A replica declares what was planted; an unplanted column may still leak by accident.
- The blind draw is a hash of the record's id against its stratum's probability. Because: Reproducible, and its probability is known before anyone labels: every blind label carries 1/p.
- Only points a reviewer can answer from what is shown are drawn, and a state field equal to the answer is hidden. Because: A value with no options stalled the queue; a revisit's state named the stage it revisited.
- Strata are whether the answers agree, not only rule against model. Because: Most studio decisions have no model answer; an override (rule against person) is the disagreement worth over-sampling.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- No replica declares its label key or family yet.
- Who labels blind is the owner's decision.

(5) How you will know it is done
- planted faults: each planted fault in the precedence, the draw, the labels and the route fails a test
- blind draw: the drawn share per stratum matches its declared probability

input:
Package 22.2: Classical decision classifiers: chosen on table folds, calibrated, each beside the rule on dev (2026-10-14).

What the package must deliver:
A pure trainer in dclab_core: candidates chosen by out-of-fold accuracy over table-grouped folds, refitted and calibrated; dev measured beside the rule; sealed rows refused. A build command writes one card per point; the fitted models are rebuilt, not committed.

The request: One classifier per decision point, trained on the generated decision sets with grouped cross-validation, calibrated, each with a card: the point, the features, the training sources, the accuracy by source and the rule's accuracy beside it.

Plan the work.
output:
(1) What the package is for
One classifier per decision point, trained on the generated decision sets with grouped cross-validation, calibrated, each with a card: the point, the features, the training sources, the accuracy by source and the rule's accuracy beside it.

(2) Plan
1. Metrics first: accuracy with an abstention counted wrong, Wilson intervals, macro figures for a choice.
2. Choose among logistic and boosted candidates by out-of-fold accuracy, folds grouped by table.
3. Refit, calibrate on the same folds, measure dev beside the rule, write the card.
4. Leave the sealed partition unread: its figures come once from the next package's gate.

(3) Decisions
- The sealed figures move to 22.3; 22.2 reports dev only, and the plan's Done-when says so. Because: 22.3 reads each sealed set once under a gate written before; reading it here first would spend it without a gate.
- A choice point's macro interval is a bootstrap clustered by table group; each class keeps its own Wilson interval. Because: A mean of ratios has no Wilson interval, and decisions of one table are not independent.
- A model's version is a hash of its candidate and its training rows. Because: Shadow answers and demotion later must tell two fitted models apart.
- The build refuses labels other than benchmark ones. Because: A measured label comes from a state field, which must be left out of the features; that list arrives with 22.4.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- The tables are generated from ten bases; real tables may have kinds these never planted.
- Measured labels need their fields left out before they can train a model.

(5) How you will know it is done
- semantic_role on dev: model accuracy above the rule's on the same dev decisions (descriptive; the promotion gate is 22.3's)
- leakage_suspect on dev: model accuracy above the rule's on the same dev decisions (descriptive)
- is_identifier on dev: model accuracy above the rule's on the same dev decisions (descriptive)

output:
(1) What the package is for
Home is where a problem becomes a solution: the user writes one sentence (or asks for any kind of model), brings data or not, and while the data is structured, cleaned and described in the background, a chat at the bottom asks a few questions about the real problem and an agent draws a solution workflow for this specific problem that follows the conversation. This package reads whatever the user brings, structured or not, into a table.

(2) Plan
1. Detect the format from the content, not the extension.
2. Write built-in readers: delimited text, Excel, Parquet, JSON (the largest list of objects), JSON lines, combined access logs, key=value logs, timestamp-level-message logs and plain text.
3. Only when no built-in reader fits, ask a model once for a regular expression; apply it to a sample, measure the parse rate and refuse a poor one.
4. Raise StructureError with a message the user can act on for unusable or oversized files.
5. Write seven small fixtures and a test per format.

(3) Decisions
- Three log patterns compete and one is used only if it reads at least half of the first 200 lines; otherwise a .log file becomes one row per line and a .txt file one row per paragraph. Because: A wrong parser that reads a quarter of the lines is worse than an honest one-row-per-line table.
- A model's pattern must match whole lines, capture at least two non-empty named fields, read at least 80% of the sample and beat the built-ins; a field's type is applied only if 95% of its values convert. Because: Code decides and a model advises: the pattern is a proposal measured on the data before it is used.
- The model sees at most 20 lines of 400 characters, and lines over 2,000 characters are skipped when applying its pattern. Because: It limits what leaves the machine and the cost of a badly written expression.
- Lists of plain values in JSON records are joined with '|'; lists of objects become an item count; objects deeper than four levels stay JSON text. Because: A record table must stay one row per record without inventing columns.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Choosing a reader by the extension misreads files saved under the wrong one (a log named .txt, a TSV named .csv).
- A model's regular expression that matches a quarter of the lines gives a table that looks parsed and is mostly wrong.
- Sending raw lines to a model to work out a format sends data the privacy text promises to keep on the machine.
- A badly written expression can hang on a long line, since Python's re has no timeout.
- Optional readers (Excel, Parquet) fail on a machine where their library is not installed.

(5) How you will know it is done
- reading speed: A large file must be read in seconds on a laptop, not minutes.

(1) What the package is for
Some users cannot share data for confidentiality; they want to simulate it from a prompt, without any sample. The rows must stay labelled synthetic everywhere.

(2) Plan
1. Write a pydantic SyntheticSpec (columns with types and distributions, a target with a type, a rate and effects) that rejects unknown fields.
2. Write generate(spec) with a seed and a row cap, and five templates (churn, fraud at 0.5%, demand as time-ordered regression, credit, maintenance).
3. With a model, design the spec from the description as JSON; validate, retry once with the error, then fall back to a template.

(3) Decisions
- A binary target's rate is calibrated exactly: a logistic latent score and the top round(rows x rate) rows positive, at least one positive. Because: Bernoulli draws after bisection can miss the asked rate by a point on small tables; the exact count keeps the same logistic model.

- Effects on identifier, text and datetime columns are refused. Because: They would plant signals no real dataset carries in that form.
- The context sent to the model drops lists of objects, frames, arrays and keys like rows, sample, preview and data, and is capped at 4,000 characters. Because: The model designs a table from the description and must never receive data rows.

- Synthetic rows lose their label somewhere (the project, the notebook, the report), and scores on invented data pass for real results.

- Rows or samples reach the model while it designs the table, though the user chose simulation to keep data private.
- A target rate that misses the asked one on a small table (fraud at 0.5%) changes the problem.
- Missingness drawn together with the target secretly carries signal.
- A silent fallback to a template gives rows that do not follow the user's description.

- synthetic flow: make product-e2e passes the synthetic flow: one prompt to a completed run of all five stages, labelled synthetic.

Plan the work.
output:
(1) What the package is for
Reuse the Evidence library's answer check (keep only sentences that cite a given record and whose numbers appear in it) for short model-written explanations of each stage record: at most 120 words, every sentence citing a claim or record id, the rest dropped. Show it on the Notebook and Reliability pages and in the brief, labelled as written by a model from the stage record, beside the unchanged deterministic notes. Never let it say production-ready.

(2) Plan
1. Look at what real stage records contain (claims and the evidence they point at) so the explanation has real material to cite.
2. Write dclab_rnd/cited.py, one shared check for model prose from records, and move the Evidence library onto it (per cited record instead of pooling all retrieved records' numbers).
3. Write studio/explain.py: the sources a model may cite come straight from the stage record (claim ids, deterministic notes, the rule records the notes cite, rules first, six at most); kept sentences are stored as record.explanation with a label and the count removed.
4. Show it, labelled, on the Notebook stage cards, the Reliability page and the brief; check the three pages on a scratch project.
5. Run check-all and the review; fix six findings; re-check; fix four more; keep A3.4's partial work set aside so A3.3 is gated and committed alone.

(3) Decisions
- One check for every piece of model prose built from records, shared with the Evidence library. Because: Two checks drift apart; a model's prose is where an invented or rounded number hides, wherever it is shown.

- Overriding a stage's choice on approve removes the explanation. Because: The explanation described the rule's pick; keeping it beside a different decision would be wrong text labelled as from the record.
- Accept that a number is checked against the sources a sentence cites, not against what it describes, and write that limit in the status row. Because: Matching numbers to subjects needs understanding the sentence; the honest move is to state the gap, not to claim more than the check proves.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- The forbidden claim ('production-ready') slipping through a negation, a Unicode variant or a synonym.
- A rounded, converted or invented number passing because the check reads digits only.
- A sentence splitter that lets an uncited sentence borrow the next sentence's citation.
- A stricter check dropping honest disclaimers and ordinary sentences.
- An explanation going stale when a person overrides the stage's choice.

output:
(1) Findings
- F1 [behaviour] A negation anywhere in the sentence let 'production-ready' through.
  Scenario: Kept: 'There is no sign of leakage, so the model is production-ready [C1].', 'It is not only accurate but production ready [C3].', 'No one doubts the model is production-ready [C1].' A bullet list '- No leakage was found\n- The model is production-ready' was one sentence and kept.
  Why it matters: 'There is no sign of leakage, so the model is production-ready' would be shown on the Notebook, Reliability and brief pages, labelled as written from the stage record: the one claim the repository forbids from benchmark evidence. The critique note and project answer had the same hole.
  Fix to ask for: A denial counts only right before the phrase (a few words at most), 'not only' excluded, with citations stripped before matching.
- F2 [behaviour] The overclaim pattern missed trivial variants of the phrase.
  Scenario: Kept: 'production  ready' (two spaces), a non-breaking space or a non-breaking hyphen between the words, 'production-\nready', 'deployment-ready', 'fit for production', 'ready to ship', 'ready to be deployed', 'can go to production'.

  Fix to ask for: Unicode is normalised and whitespace collapsed before matching; the pattern covers production or deployment ready, readiness, grade, quality, fit for production, ready to ship or be deployed, go live or to production.
- F3 [behaviour] A number without a leading zero, or glued to letters, was not read, so an invented number survived.
  Scenario: 'The model scored .99 on the holdout [C1]' while the claim says 0.9248: kept. 'AUC0.99' and '~.99' gave no numbers. The text cleaner also turned the kept text into 'scored.99'.
  Why it matters: 'The model scored .99 on the holdout' would be kept beside a claim of 0.9248, so a person would read an invented score as checked against the record.
  Fix to ask for: Numbers such as .99 and AUC0.99 are read; the cleaner removes only spaces before a final stop or comma.
- F4 [behaviour] The sentence splitter did not split before a lowercase word or at a line break, so an uncited sentence rode on the next one's citation.
  Scenario: 'The model is safe, fair and ready to ship. extra_trees scored 0.9248 on the holdout [A].' was kept whole, cited to A; bullets merged, so a number in one bullet passed on another bullet's source.

  Fix to ask for: Split at a stop followed by whitespace and at line breaks; fragments fail closed.
- F5 [behaviour] Numbers were compared as digits only.

  Why it matters: A model could write '61%' or '61 million rows' where the record says 61 rows, or drop a minus sign so a loss reads as a gain, and the check would keep it.
  Fix to ask for: Numbers keep their unit and their sign when the sentence writes one; number words are read as digits or must be words of a cited source; the gap that numbers are checked against cited sources, not subjects, is written in the status row.

  Scenario: The features stage selects recipe X and the explanation says so; the person approves with choice Y; the Notebook card and the brief still say X beside the changed decision.
  Why it matters: After the person overrode a stage's choice, the Notebook card and the brief still explained the rule's pick, so a reader of the brief would see a recipe that was not used.
  Fix to ask for: When the approved choice overrides the rule's selection, the explanation is removed.
- R1 [behaviour] The overclaim filter rewrote text even when it removed nothing (a regression).
  Scenario: A critique 'Risks:\n- Leakage is possible\n- Small sample\n- Check the time split' came back as one flattened line with count 0.
  Why it matters: Every critique note and project answer written as a list came back flattened into one line even with nothing removed, so the fix for F4 degraded every structured answer.
  Fix to ask for: The original text is returned when nothing is removed; otherwise line breaks are kept.
- R2 [behaviour] A stop with no space after it still merged an uncited sentence.
  Scenario: 'The model is safe and fair.It scored 0.9248 [A].' was kept whole, uncited claim included.
  Why it matters: 'The model is safe and fair.It scored 0.9248 [A].' kept the uncited first half as if [A] supported it.
  Fix to ask for: A stop glued to a capital also ends a sentence (and, after A3.4's review, not when it is the dot of a code name such as pd.DataFrame).
- R3 [behaviour] Two denial idioms still let 'production-ready' through.
  Scenario: 'It is not just production-ready.' and 'It is without doubt production-ready.' were kept.
  Why it matters: 'It is without doubt production-ready' would be shown, the strongest form of the forbidden claim.
  Fix to ask for: 'not just', 'not merely' and 'not simply' are excluded, and 'without doubt' or 'without question' is not a denial.
- R4 [gap] The stricter check dropped natural disclaimers and ordinary sentences.
  Scenario: 'This does not mean the model is ready for production.' and 'Benchmark evidence should not be treated as production-ready.' were dropped (the denial window was two words), so the final stage's caveat was the sentence most likely lost; 'ten folds' was dropped against '10 folds'; 'claim C1' in prose was dropped as a number.
  Why it matters: The caveat the final-stage prompt asks for ('This does not mean the model is ready for production') would be removed, so explanations would lose exactly the limit they exist to state.
  Fix to ask for: The denial window is four words; count words are read as digits with their unit; a name with digits is hidden only when a cited source writes it.

(2) Verdict
FAIL: 10 findings to fix before this change is committed.

Package A4.3: Prompts as code: versioned files pinned to a complete suite run (2026-10-06).

What the package must deliver:
A change to a policy prompt, a tool schema or a validator rule must pass the scripted suite; the live results of the last release are the baseline to compare. Done when a test fails when a prompt file changes without its recorded hash being updated by the suite run.

The request: Treat prompts as code with tests. Keep each policy's system prompt and tool schemas in versioned files; record a hash of each next to the latest scripted-suite result; make rd-check fail when a prompt or schema changed and the suite has not been re-run for that hash; when a live baseline exists, print the change in score per case after a run. No prompt text is edited by a model.

Plan the work.
output:
(1) What the package is for
Treat prompts as code with tests. Keep each policy's system prompt and tool schemas in versioned files; record a hash of each next to the latest scripted-suite result; make rd-check fail when a prompt or schema changed and the suite has not been re-run for that hash; when a live baseline exists, print the change in score per case after a run. No prompt text is edited by a model.

(2) Plan
1. Find every prompt DCLab sends to a model: ten, as string constants in their modules (intern, home_agent, home_plan, synthetic_schema, parse_pattern, stage_critique, stage_explain, leakage_review, notebook_fixes, evidence_answer).
2. Move each into dclab_rnd/prompts/<name>.md, read with prompts.text(name); a number a prompt states becomes a placeholder filled from the module's constant; compare every prompt byte for byte before and after.
3. Write prompts.fingerprints() over the prompt files and each tool scope's schemas; store it with every scripted run (AEV-003); write tests/test_prompt_gate.py; make live runs compare with a baseline.
4. Run check-all and the review; fix four findings; rerun the suite (a failed run turned out to be the disk filling again); commit.

(3) Decisions
- The move must change no prompt: each module's text is compared byte for byte before and after. Because: A refactor of prompts that changes a word changes behaviour with no test noticing, the very risk the package removes.
- Only a complete scripted run (every policy on every case, no errors) stores the hashes. Because: Otherwise a partial run, or one where every case errors, satisfies the gate while the suite has not passed.
- The campaign tool's schema is hashed by its name, description and fields, not by pydantic's generated JSON schema. Because: The generated schema depends on the installed pydantic version, so the gate would flip between machines with no repository change.
- The gate asks for a rerun, not for the scores to hold. Because: A score drop after a prompt change is for a person to judge; the gate's job is to make sure the change was measured.
- A test keeps code from writing the prompt files. Because: People edit prompts; no tool or model may.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Moving prompts into files changing a word or a newline that no test notices.
- A gate satisfied by any file carrying the right hash, including a partial or failing run.
- Hashes of library-generated schemas that flip between machines with no repository change.
- Live score changes printed against a baseline that ran on different cases.
- Prompts left in their modules, outside the gate.

(5) How you will know it is done
- AEV-003, scripted suite rerun after moving the prompts: The move changes no prompt (byte-identical), so the complete scripted run must give the same scorecard as AEV-001.

Package RD-expansion-v1: The task-type expansion: imbalanced fraud, 26 classes, a time series and text with tables (2026-10-03).

What the package must deliver:
dclab_rnd/expansion/ and evidence/campaigns/expansion_v1: 20 experiments (EXP-051 to EXP-070), four real public datasets x the same five stages, with a task-aware split, metric, leakage heuristics, recipes, model families, bootstrap and naive baselines; raw files downloaded on first use with pinned SHA-256; results in the binary campaign's schema plus task_type, primary_metric and setup_summary.

The request: The 50-experiment campaign covered binary classification only. Add Kaggle and Hugging Face style data and the missing task types (multiclass, time series, imbalanced fraud, text plus tabular) with the same evidence discipline.

Plan the work.
output:
(1) What the package is for
The 50-experiment campaign covered binary classification only. Add Kaggle and Hugging Face style data and the missing task types (multiclass, time series, imbalanced fraud, text plus tabular) with the same evidence discipline.

(2) Plan
1. Pick one real dataset per task type: credit-card fraud (284,807 rows, 0.17% positive), letter recognition (20,000 rows, 26 classes), daily bike sharing (728 days), women's clothing reviews (23,486 reviews with text).
2. Write each dataset's decision-time contract and holdout policy: last 20% by time for fraud and bike, stratified 20% for letters, unseen Clothing ID groups for reviews.
3. Select on training rows only with time-ordered, stratified or grouped 3-fold CV; read the holdout once in stage 5.
4. Make leakage heuristics task-aware (univariate signal, exact proxies, a + b == target identities, uniqueness) with synthetic canaries; measure safe vs unsafe CV and, for bike, random vs time-ordered CV.
5. Compare each holdout with naive baselines and, for fraud, apply a threshold chosen on training out-of-fold scores.
6. Fold the results into the critic gate, the evidence index, the blind auditor replay and SFT v3.

(3) Decisions
- Download from GitHub mirrors and pin each file's SHA-256; a mismatch stops the run. Because: Kaggle, Hugging Face and UCI were blocked from the cloud environment; pinning the hash makes the mirror's file the one the results describe.
- For fraud, fit models on all positives and a seeded 25% of negatives, but validate and score the holdout on every row, correcting probabilities back to the true base rate. Because: It keeps 284,807-row CV affordable while metrics, thresholds and calibration stay on the real distribution.
- Give tree models the top 2,000 chi-squared TF-IDF columns, selected inside each fit fold; linear models see the full matrix. Because: Trees cannot use 30,000 sparse columns cheaply, and selecting outside the folds would be PIT-002's mistake.
- Copy the binary campaign's conventions into the expansion package instead of importing dclab_rnd.science. Because: science could not be imported in that environment because general_pipeline needs catboost.
- Block the clothing reviews' Positive Feedback Count as well as Rating. Because: Helpful votes accrue after the review is published, even though the measured lift was only +0.0001.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- A random split on daily data, so the model trains on days after the ones it is scored on.
- Judging a fraud problem with 0.17% positives by accuracy, where always answering 'not fraud' looks excellent.
- Selecting text features outside the folds, repeating PIT-002's mistake on tens of thousands of sparse columns.
- Downloading from a mirror that serves a different file from the one the results describe.
- Same-day parts of a regression target shipped as features, so the target is rebuilt rather than predicted.

(5) How you will know it is done
- credit-card fraud, average precision: Choices on time-ordered training CV; tuning accepted only above a 0.005 AP margin; holdout (last 20% by time) read once with a bootstrap interval; compared with random ranking.
- letter recognition, macro-F1: Stratified CV; recipe within 0.002 of the best; tuning accepted above 0.002; holdout read once.
- bike sharing, MAE: Expanding-window time-ordered CV; tuning accepted above a declared margin; holdout (last 146 days) read once with a moving-block bootstrap; compared with lag-2, lag-7 and mean baselines.

The request: Make paired instruction data an SFT job can train on directly, cleaner than v1, and show how to run the training job.

output:
(1) What the package is for
Make paired instruction data an SFT job can train on directly, cleaner than v1, and show how to run the training job.

(2) Plan
1. Give every example a dataset card (what the data predicts), a stage card (what the stage does) and a setup summary (what was compared in that run).
2. Build seven tasks: grounded QA, explain an experiment, critique a claim, apply a selection rule, judge leakage, reason with a rule, and workflow steps.
3. Drop critic challenges the gate contradicts; reject examples with a path, hash or excessive length.
4. Hold out heart_disease, spambase and the clothing reviews entirely; split dataset-free examples by hash.
5. Write the LoRA trainer and the deterministic evaluator; check the evaluator scores the reference answers 1.0.

(3) Decisions
- Hold out whole datasets for validation. Because: Examples from the same dataset are near-duplicates; a random split would measure memory, not reasoning.
- Put the evidence in the prompt (RAFT-style). Because: The model should learn to reason from given evidence, which retrieval will supply in use, rather than recite facts.
- Score with a deterministic evaluator, not an LLM judge. Because: A judge model adds its own errors to the measurement.

(4) Risks to check before calling it done
- Examples that leave out the evidence their answer depends on, so the model learns to recite.
- A random split that puts near-duplicate examples from one dataset in both training and validation.
- Critic challenges contradicted by the numbers entering the training data.
- Paths, hashes or machine details in the examples.
- An LLM judge in the evaluator adding its own errors to the score.

- corpus v3 build: Whole datasets held out; contradicted challenges dropped; no example with a path, hash or excess length.

What the package must deliver:
build_sft_dataset_v3.py writing RAFT-style examples (the evidence the answer depends on is in the prompt) in chat, Alpaca and ShareGPT formats, with whole datasets held out for validation; quality gates against paths, hashes and contradicted critic claims; train_lora.py (TRL with LoRA) and eval_sft.py (deterministic scoring, no LLM judge); docs/guides/SFT_DATA_GUIDE.md.

The change: research/llm-fine-tuning/experiments/sft/build_sft_dataset_v3.py, out_v3/ (examples and MANIFEST.json), train_lora.py, eval_sft.py and the SFT guide; make sft-v3 and a freshness check.

A finding (owner, behaviour): Examples asked about an experiment id without saying what the experiment was.
How it shows: A v1 example asked 'What did experiment EXP-023 on the credit_default dataset find during the feature engineering stage?' and answered 'Use the raw feature recipe ... 0.7317 mean training-CV ROC-AUC' without saying what credit_default predicts, what the stage does or what was compared. (1) Root cause
The v1 builder turned claim-memory lines into questions and kept only their ids as context.

(2) Why it matters

It changes what DCLab does for a person without anyone deciding it: a result, a refusal or an artefact differs from what the person was promised, silently.

(3) The smallest fix
Every v3 example carries the dataset card, the stage card and the run's setup summary, all taken from the records, never invented.

(4) The test that proves it
No dedicated test was recorded for this fix: write one that reproduces the scenario above and fails before the change.

(5) What stays open
Nothing beyond the scenario, once the test passes.

Switch the product's models from OpenAI to Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5; keep collecting training data without training; confirm retention (events 24 months, model text 12), readers of sessions (owner and admin) and blind labelling (the owner first), and show how to label.

- The research campaign still needs an OpenAI-compatible key.

- tests: the model tests and the new transport tests pass with no live call
